title: psdk komak
description: A cross-platform Flutter app for learning small things in small moments, through short decks of cards and seven different ways of being quizzed on them.

Overview.What Is psdk komak:
psdk komak is built around one idea: some things are too small to sit down and study, but big enough that you'd like to actually know them one day. Capital cities, the order of the months, a handful of new words in a language you're picking up. This app is for the minute you have while a kettle boils, a bus is late, or you're waiting for anything at all.

## The three building blocks

- **Deck** — a themed collection of cards, e.g. *World Capitals* or *Months Of The Year*.
- **Card** — one small fact, always with a **front** (the prompt) and a **back** (the answer).
- **Session** — a short mixed round pulling cards from a deck and asking about them in one of several ways.

## Repeating, not memorizing

psdk komak deliberately does not use a strict spaced-repetition schedule with due dates. The goal isn't to cram something into long-term memory on a fixed timetable — it's to keep bumping into the same small set of facts often enough that they stick naturally. Cards you've seen less recently, or gotten wrong more often, show up more, but there's no pressure, no overdue count, and no guilt for skipping a day. See [The Repetition Model](/psdk-komak/architecture-repetition-model/) for how this is calculated.
Overview.Platforms And Storage:
psdk komak runs on Android, Linux and Windows from one Flutter codebase.

- **Storage** is local only, via `shared_preferences` — everything you add lives on the device you added it on. There is no account and no sync between devices.
- **Theming** uses [Catppuccin](https://github.com/catppuccin/catppuccin): Latte for light mode, Mocha for dark mode.
- **Typography** is Space Grotesk for Latin-script text, with Noto Sans fallbacks for Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Thai and Simplified Chinese, so cards in other scripts and languages render properly without extra setup.
- **Sound** is optional and can be switched off entirely in Settings.

Question Types.How Question Types Work:
Every question type in psdk komak is generated automatically from a deck's existing cards — you never author a "multiple choice card" or an "order card" directly. Instead, a small number of optional fields on an ordinary card unlock extra question types for the whole deck:

| Field | Unlocks |
| --- | --- |
| *(none — just front/back)* | Flip Review, Multiple Choice, Timed Recall, Type The Answer |
| `orderIndex` (a number, set on 3+ cards) | Correct Order |
| `groupId` (a shared label, set on 2+ groups of cards) | Find The Odd One Out |

Matching just needs four or more cards in the deck; there's no extra field to fill in.

You can turn individual question types on or off per deck from the deck's menu, in case a particular deck only makes sense as flashcards, or only as an order quiz.
Question Types.Flip Review:
The classic flip card. You see the front, tap it to flip to the back, and then rate how well you remembered it: **Again**, **Hard**, **Good** or **Easy**.

- **Again** and **Hard** count as a miss for that card.
- **Good** and **Easy** count as a hit.

This is the only question type that works for absolutely any card, so it's the fallback used whenever a deck has no other question types enabled.
Question Types.Multiple Choice:
You're shown a card's front and four possible answers — the real one plus three distractors pulled at random from other cards in the same deck. Pick one; the right answer lights up either way so you always see the correct pairing before moving on.

Needs at least four cards in the deck so there are enough distractors to pull from.
Question Types.Timed Recall:
The same layout as Multiple Choice, but with a shrinking progress bar giving you roughly eight seconds to answer. Running out of time counts as a miss, the same as picking the wrong option.

Meant to add a little pressure for decks you already know reasonably well — it's more fun than useful for a deck you're only just starting.
Question Types.Type The Answer: You see the front and type the back from memory instead of picking it from a list. The check is forgiving: it trims whitespace, ignores case, and collapses repeated spaces, so "  Paris" and "paris" both count as correct, but it does expect the wording to match — useful for names, dates and vocabulary, less useful for anything with many equally valid phrasings.
Question Types.Correct Order:
A handful of cards from the deck are shown in a shuffled pile; tap them in what you believe is the correct sequence. Order is determined by each card's `orderIndex` — the built-in *Months Of The Year* deck is the reference example, with January through December numbered 1 to 12.

Only cards that have an `orderIndex` set take part; if fewer than three cards in a deck have one, Correct Order stays unavailable for that deck.
Question Types.Match The Pairs: Two columns appear: fronts on the left in a fixed order, backs on the right shuffled. Tap one on each side to try a pair — correct pairs lock in place, wrong ones briefly flash and reset. The round finishes once every pair is matched; getting there without any wrong attempts counts as a full hit for every card involved, and any mistake along the way counts the whole round as a miss (though you still finish it).
Question Types.Find The Odd One Out:
A small grid of cards appears — most share a `groupId` (for example, "fruit"), and exactly one comes from a different group. Tap the one that doesn't belong.

Needs at least two distinct group labels used across four or more cards in the deck. The built-in *Spot The Imposter* deck (fruits, vegetables and fish) is the reference example.

Adding Cards.Ways To Add Cards:
There are four ways to get cards into a deck, from quickest to most involved:

1. **Paste multiple as CSV** — for when you already have a short list somewhere and just want it in fast.
2. **Import from a file or link** — for anything bigger, or anything you already have as a `.json`, `.csv` or `.txt` file, including files hosted somewhere online.
3. **Add one by one** — the manual editor, best for a card or two, or for filling in `orderIndex`/`groupId` precisely.
4. **Built-in decks** — *Months Of The Year*, *World Capitals* and *Spot The Imposter* ship with the app so there's something to try immediately.
Adding Cards.Manual Entry:
The single-card editor has four fields:

- **Front** and **Back** — required, plain text (multi-line is fine).
- **Order position** — optional; fill this in on every card in a deck to unlock Correct Order.
- **Group label** — optional; give two or more cards the same label, across at least two different labels, to unlock Find The Odd One Out.

Editing an existing card reuses the same screen, pre-filled.
Adding Cards.Bulk CSV Paste:
Open a deck and choose **Paste multiple as CSV**. It's a single large text box: one card per line, `front,back`, with two optional trailing columns for `orderIndex` and `groupId`. A header row (`front,back,orderIndex,groupId`) is optional and detected automatically if the first cell contains the word "front".

```
front,back
Capital of France,Paris
Capital of Japan,Tokyo
```

The preview below the text box updates as you type, showing exactly how many cards will be added and flagging any line it couldn't parse, before you commit anything.
Adding Cards.Importing A File Or Link:
The **Import** screen (reachable from the home screen's **New** button, or from inside any deck) supports three sources:

- **Paste** — the same JSON/CSV/`=:=` text parsers as everywhere else, for pasting content from elsewhere.
- **File** — pick a `.json`, `.csv` or `.txt` file already on the device.
- **Link** — fetch a URL that responds with JSON, CSV or plain text.

Whichever source you use, once parsed you'll see how many cards were found and how many lines were skipped, then choose whether to create a brand new deck from them or add them into the deck you opened Import from.
Adding Cards.Importing From A Link:
For the **Link** source, the response's `Content-Type` header decides how the body is read:

- Anything containing `json` → parsed as JSON.
- Anything containing `csv` → parsed as CSV.
- Anything else falls back to sniffing the URL's file extension, then the content itself (JSON if it starts with `{` or `[`, `=:=` text if that separator appears, otherwise CSV).

Responses are capped at 5 MB and a 15 second timeout, mostly to fail fast and clearly rather than to hang.
Adding Cards.The =:= Text Format:
The plain-text import format uses a three-character separator, `=:=`, chosen because it's vanishingly unlikely to appear in ordinary text by accident:

```
Capital of France=:=Paris
Capital of Japan=:=Tokyo
```

Each line is one card: everything before the first `=:=` is the front, everything after is the back. Because a real line break always starts a new card, an intentional line break *inside* a front or back is written as the two literal characters `\n` (backslash, then the letter n) rather than an actual newline — psdk komak converts that sequence back into a real line break when reading the field, and does the reverse when exporting a deck back out to this format.

Customization.Themes:
Settings offers two things about appearance:

- **Match system theme** (on by default) — the app follows your device's light/dark setting, using Catppuccin Latte for light and Mocha for dark.
- Turning that off reveals a manual **Latte / Mocha** picker instead, if you'd like one fixed regardless of the system setting.
Customization.Text Size And Motion:
- **Text size** is a slider from 85% to 135%, applied app-wide, for anyone who prefers larger or smaller text than the device default.
- **Reduce motion** trims transition and entrance animations down to something quicker and simpler, for anyone sensitive to motion or who just prefers a snappier feel.
Customization.Sound: Small sound effects play on key moments — a tap, a correct answer, a wrong answer, a card flip, finishing a session — and can be switched off entirely with one toggle in Settings if you'd rather study in silence.

Architecture.Data Model:
Every question type is generated from one shared card shape rather than needing its own data structure:

```json
{
  "front": "January",
  "back": "Month 1 of 12 — 31 days",
  "orderIndex": 1,
  "groupId": null
}
```

`orderIndex` and `groupId` are both optional and both `null` on an ordinary card. A deck becomes eligible for Correct Order once three or more of its cards carry an `orderIndex`, and eligible for Find The Odd One Out once its cards span two or more distinct `groupId` values across four or more cards. This is what lets one flat list of cards support seven different question types without a separate authoring format for each one.
Architecture.The Repetition Model: Rather than scheduling cards against calculated due-dates, each card simply tracks how many times it's been shown, how many of those were correct, and when it was last shown. Building a session picks cards with a weighted random draw: cards seen very recently are strongly deprioritized, cards not seen in a while are favored, and cards with a lower running accuracy are favored as well. The randomness is deliberate — the point is a good chance of seeing the cards that need it most, not a rigid, predictable order.
